newsitem.title: GERMANY: Depressed Bunds draw little cheer from T-bonds.
newsitem.headline: Depressed Bunds draw little cheer from T-bonds.

text.p: German debt prices spent most of Monday's session firmly anchored under water, dragged down by a struggling currency and persistent worries about the outlook for interest rates.

Even a firmer start to Treasuries largely failed to induce a better mood in Bunds, with the DTB September futures contract nudging reluctantly two basis points up on the day to 102.92 in late trade -- its first attempt at gains this session.
Analysts predicted a week of underperformance in the German market with U.S. Treasuries likely to outpace Bunds amid a barrage of U.S. economic data.
Some said the 10-year yield spread between the two markets, which was at 70 basis points at 1424 GMT, could tighten to 60 basis points in the near term.
"Bunds are looking pretty uncomfortable, but they will be helped if the U.S. market finds a reason in this week's numbers to rally," said one Frankfurt-based trader.
Among a flood of other numbers, U.S. second quarter GDP and the July employment report are slated for release this week.
But analysts said domestic concerns would continue to weigh on the German market, limiting any Bund gains.

The mark -- which reached its lowest point for seven-and-a-half years in Tokyo overnight -- is the market's main worry as its weakness fuels talk that the Bundesbank may consider moving to a variable repo rate.
Analysts said that unless the mark stages an unexpected turnaround against the dollar, such speculation will grow and continue to unnerve Bund investors.

Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Broethers in Frankfurt said that if the mark were to fall further -- say to around 1.90 marks to the dollar -- the Bundesbank probably would make the switch from the fixed to a variable repo.
Analysts also said the substantial yield curve flattening seen late last week was likely to continue in the medium term, although the pace of the change would slow somewhat.
"We've seen the long end hit a bit more today and selling at the short end ease off," said one. "So in fact the curve has steepened slightly after the flattening we saw last week."

But he added that the general trend of heavy pressure on shorter dated paper would continue as long as the mark remained weak, while longer-dated paper would remain relatively unharmed by the currency's weakness.
